procedural_history.originating_court: Special Judge (conviction and sentencing of imprisonment)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment of the Judicial Commissioner of Vindhya Pradesh setting aside the acquittal of the petitioner, convicting him, and imposing a sentence of imprisonment.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The petitioner appealed to the Court of the Judicial Commissioner of Vindhya Pradesh, which set aside the acquittal and convicted the petitioner.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that his imprisonment was not in accordance with procedure established by law. He raised two main points: (1) that the Court of the Judicial Commissioner lacked jurisdiction to hear the appeal from the Special Judge (this point was not pressed), and (2) that his appeal in the Supreme Court against the Judicial Commissioner's judgment should have been heard and completely disposed of by a Constitution Bench under Article 145(3).

issue.issue_text: Whether Article 145(3) of the Constitution requires that a case, which at any stage involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, must be heard and decided in its entirety by a Constitution Bench of at least five judges.

law.fact_text: Article 145(3) of the Constitution mandates that the minimum number of judges required to decide any case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution shall be five.

application.fact_text: The petitioner argued that once a case is identified as involving a substantial constitutional question, the entire case, in all its aspects, must be heard and decided by a Constitution Bench of at least five judges. They contended that the words "the case" in the article are indivisible.

The Court rejected this interpretation, reasoning that the underlying principle of the Constitution is to ensure that the *constitutional questions themselves* are decided by a bench of at least five judges.

The Court found that splitting a case into different stages is not repugnant to the Constitution or procedural law. It pointed to the proviso of Article 145(3) and Article 228, which explicitly contemplate separating constitutional questions from the rest of the case for decision by a specific bench.

The Court held that its power to split the case is inherent. It interpreted Article 145(3) as requiring five judges to sit only "in so far and as long as" the case involves the substantial constitutional question.

The Court also relied on its established practice (cursus curiae est lex curiae), where a Constitution Bench decides the constitutional issues and then leaves the other subsidiary questions to be disposed of by a smaller Division Bench in conformity with the Constitution Bench's opinion. This practice saves the time of the larger bench.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's contention, holding that Article 145(3) does not require the entire case to be decided by a Constitution Bench. The constitutional mandate is fulfilled as long as the substantial questions of law regarding the interpretation of the Constitution are decided by a bench of at least five judges. The rest of the case can then be competently decided by a smaller Division Bench.

issue.issue_text: Whether a case can be heard 'piecemeal', with the substantial questions of constitutional law being decided by a Constitution Bench and the remaining parts of the case being decided by a smaller bench.

law.law_text: The underlying principle of the Constitution is that all substantial questions of law regarding the interpretation of the Constitution must be heard and decided by a Bench of not less than five Judges (a 'Constitution Bench').

The splitting of cases into different stages for hearing and decision is not repugnant to the Constitution or the general principles of procedural law, as evidenced by provisions like Article 228 of the Constitution and sections of the Codes of Civil and Criminal Procedure.
Article 145(3) and its proviso make a distinction between a 'case' and a 'question' of constitutional importance, which implies that the two can be separated.

application.application_text: The Court reasoned that as long as the core constitutional requirement—that constitutional questions are decided by a bench of at least five judges—is fulfilled, there is no constitutional objection to the rest of the case being handled by a smaller bench.

The Court interpreted the words 'the case' as not being indivisible. Once the Constitution Bench decides the constitutional questions, the remainder of the case can no longer be described as 'a case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution'.

The Court drew an analogy to Article 228, which allows a High Court to withdraw a case from a lower court, decide the constitutional question, and then return the case to the original court for final disposal. This demonstrates that the principle of splitting a case is already accepted within the constitutional framework.
The Court also noted the practical benefit of this procedure, as it saves the time of the Constitution Bench, allowing it to focus solely on matters of constitutional importance.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that it is competent and constitutionally permissible to split up a case. A Constitution Bench can decide the substantial questions of constitutional law, and the rest of the case can then be dealt with and disposed of by a smaller Division Bench in conformity with the opinion of the Constitution Bench.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Article 145(3) of the Constitution requires that a case, which at any stage involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, must be heard and decided in its entirety by a Constitution Bench of at least five judges.
appellant_arguments: If a case involves a substantial question of constitutional interpretation, the entire case must be heard and decided by a Constitution Bench of at least five judges.
Interpreting a 'case' to mean a 'part of a case' would render the main provision of Article 145(3) nugatory.
The specific legal provisions that allow for splitting a case are exceptions to a general rule of indivisibility, and their very existence proves that splitting is not otherwise permitted.
Consequently, a judgment on the non-constitutional parts of such a case by a smaller bench is illegal and void.
respondent_arguments: Article 145(3) and its proviso should be read together, which allows for a flexible procedure.
A 'case' can be interpreted to mean a 'part of a case,' allowing the constitutional questions to be separated from the rest of the matter.
The practice of hearing a case in parts is contemplated in other procedural laws, such as the Codes of Civil and Criminal Procedure, showing it is a permissible practice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a case can be heard 'piecemeal', with the substantial questions of constitutional law being decided by a Constitution Bench and the remaining parts of the case being decided by a smaller bench.
appellant_arguments: A case cannot be heard 'piecemeal' by different benches unless it falls under a specific exception, such as the proviso to Article 145(3).

The proviso to Article 145(3) makes a clear distinction between a 'case' and a 'question,' implying that only a specific question can be referred to a larger bench, not that the case itself can be split for hearing by different benches.

Analogies to procedural codes are irrelevant because those codes deal with courts of co-ordinate jurisdiction, whereas here the very competency of the smaller bench to hear any part of the case is in question.
respondent_arguments: Splitting up a case for hearing by different benches is a permissible procedure.
The substantial questions of constitutional law can be decided by a Constitution Bench, while the remaining parts of the case can be validly decided by a smaller bench.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Article 145(3) of the Constitution requires that a minimum of five judges must sit for the purpose of deciding a case only to the extent that it involves a substantial question of law regarding the interpretation of the Constitution. Once such constitutional questions have been decided by a bench of five or more judges, the rest of the case can be disposed of by a smaller bench.
obiter: The splitting of cases into different stages for hearing and decision is not repugnant to the Constitution or general principles of procedural law, as indicated by provisions such as Article 228.
The practice of the court is the law of the court (cursus curiae est lex curiae).
The Constitution distinguishes between the decision of the 'case itself' and a 'question of law' of constitutional importance involved in that case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court construed clause (3) of Article 145 as requiring only that the minimum number of five Judges must sit for the purpose of deciding any case in so far and as long as it involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution. Once the constitutional questions are disposed of by the Constitution Bench, the remaining parts of the case can be heard and decided by a smaller Division Bench, as the case can no longer be described as one involving a substantial question of constitutional interpretation.
legal_tests_applied: Purposive Interpretation: The Court identified the "underlying principle of the Constitution" which "is clear and all that it insists upon is that all constitutional questions should be heard and decided by a Bench of not Jess than five Judges."

Cursus Curiae Est Lex Curiae: The Court relied on the maxim that the practice of the court is the law of the court, stating, "it is on this interpretation that the practice has grown up in this Court for a Constitution Bench to dispose of all constitutional questions and to leave the other subsidiary questions for disposal by a Divisron Bench... There is nothing that we find in the body of clause (3) of article 145 which compels us to depart from the famous maxim cursus curiae est lex curiae."
why_appellant_lost: The Court rejected the appellant's argument that specific provisions allowing for the splitting of cases are exceptions that prove a general rule of indivisibility. Instead, the Court found that provisions like the proviso to Article 145(3) and Article 228 "quite clearly indicate that the splitting up of cases into different stages for hearing and decisions is not repugnant to the Constitution or the general principles of procedural law."

The Court disagreed that interpreting 'case' as 'part of a case' would render Article 145(3) nugatory. It reasoned that a case's character is not static; once the constitutional questions are decided by a Constitution Bench, "what remains of the case cannot properly or appropriately be described as still a 'case involving a substantial question of law· as to the interpretation of this Constitution'."

The Court found no inherent quality of indivisibility in the term 'the case' as used in Article 145(3), concluding that "in construing clause (3) of article 145 no quality of indivisibility need be attributed to the words 'the case' used therein."
why_respondent_won: The Court found that the Constitution itself contemplates the splitting of cases, noting that the proviso to Article 145(3) and Article 228 make a distinction between deciding a 'case' and deciding a 'question' of constitutional law, thereby permitting the constitutional question to be decided by a larger bench while the rest of the case is handled by a smaller one.

The Court reasoned that a case's nature can change during proceedings. "A case may, to begin with, involve a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, but it may cease to do so at a later stage," such as when the constitutional questions are decided or when counsel chooses not to press them.

The Court affirmed its inherent power to manage its proceedings, stating, "If a Court is entitled to decide a case in stages, as the Privy Council has held it can, there is no reason why article 145(3) should· be so construed as to deprive this.Court of that inherent power."

The Court's established practice of having a Constitution Bench decide constitutional questions and a Division Bench decide the remainder was held to be a valid interpretation of the law under the maxim 'cursus curiae est lex curiae'.
policy_considerations: The Court was motivated by judicial efficiency, noting that its interpretation allows for the rest of the case to be disposed of by a smaller bench "so as to save the time of the Constitution Bench of five or more Judges."

The Court considered the practical absurdity of the appellant's position through a hypothetical: "Suppose a case which involves a constitutional question is placed before a Constitution Bench but learned counsel appearing in support of the case intimates to the Bench that he does not press any constitutional point, surely he cannot, in that situation, insist that the time of a Bench of five or more Judges should be spent on the determination of a case which, by his own election, has ceased· to involve any constitutional question."
